article_title: Motor sequences resist automatization as attentional demands increase with sequence learning
citation: Dahm, S. F., Kraft, V., Martini, M., Krause, D. & Hermsdoerfer, J. (2026). Motor sequences resist automatization as attentional demands increase with sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00412-y
title: Parallel-Neural-Network-Model account: attentional demands increase in the transition from the reacting mode to the associative mode during sequence learning
description: The article applies the Parallel-Neural-Network-Model, in which a fast-learning, attention-dependent spatial system and a slow-learning motor system operate in parallel, and sequence execution proceeds through a reacting mode, an associative mode, and a chunking mode. The authors interpret their counterintuitive finding that dual-task costs increased for the practiced sequence within this framework: "sequence production based on explicit internal sequence representations (i.e., associative mode) requires more attentional resources than reacting to external stimulus information (i.e., reacting mode)". They also invoke the Triarchic Theory of Learning, predicting automaticity develops only after a temporary increase in attentional demands.
requirements: Extensive practice of a fixed sequence before automatization is expected
Assessment of automatization via comparison of dual-task and single-task performance
constraints: The article states progression to the automatic mode may require even more extensive practice than the ten sessions used
Sequence complexity may moderate automatization effects, with shorter sequences automatized after relatively little practice
target_learners: Adults learning motor sequences (participants aged 19 to 35)
target_learning_goals: Automatization of motor sequences and reduction of attentional demands during skilled performance
examples: The study contrasted a ten-session practiced sequence against an unpracticed structurally matched control sequence under single- and dual-task conditions
key_sources: Dahm, S. F., Kraft, V., Martini, M., Krause, D. & Hermsdoerfer, J. (2026). Motor sequences resist automatization as attentional demands increase with sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00412-y

article_title: A Quantitative Analysis of Language Interventions for Children with Autism
citation: Kane, M., Connell, J. E., & Pellecchia, M. (2008). A Quantitative Analysis of Language Interventions for Children with Autism. The Behavior Analyst Today, 11(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Quantitative+Analysis+of+Language+Interventions+for+Children+with+Autism
title: Percentage of non-overlapping data (PND) with Scruggs and Mastropieri effectiveness cutoffs
description: PND is a non-parametric measure for evaluating single-subject research, calculated by dividing the number of treatment-phase data points exceeding the highest baseline data point by the total treatment data points and multiplying by 100. The article applies Scruggs and Mastropieri (1998) cutoffs: "very effective treatments (over 90 PND), effective treatments (between 70 and 90 PND), questionable effectiveness (between 50 and 70 PND), and ineffective treatments (below 50 PND)." Inter-observer agreement for PND calculations in this meta-analysis was 90.2%.
requirements: Each study must present a graphic display of the data in order for PND values to be calculated.
constraints: PND has been criticized in the literature for not representing treatment outcomes accurately (Allison & Gorman, 1994; Levin, 1992), though the authors argue it is easily computed and interpretable.
target_learners: Children aged 2-13 diagnosed with autism, PDD, or PDD-NOS
target_learning_goals: Evaluating effectiveness of spoken language acquisition interventions
examples: The authors calculated 103 PND scores for contrived interventions and 49 for naturalistic interventions across the 22 included studies.
key_sources: Kane, M., Connell, J. E., & Pellecchia, M. (2008). A Quantitative Analysis of Language Interventions for Children with Autism. The Behavior Analyst Today, 11(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=A+Quantitative+Analysis+of+Language+Interventions+for+Children+with+Autism

article_title: Pilot Simulation Task Trainer for Prehospital Management of Neck Hemorrhage.
citation: Sussman S, Melaragno L, Nisenbaum E, Malara M, Herster R, Orban C, Marquardt M, Haring C, Harmon K, VanKoevering K. (2026). Pilot Simulation Task Trainer for Prehospital Management of Neck Hemorrhage. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.47912
title: Three-step prehospital algorithm for vascular neck injury: identify, control, transfer
description: The article proposes a simplified prehospital treatment algorithm for penetrating neck injury consisting of "1) identify primarily venous vs high-volume arterial bleeding; 2) control the hemorrhage; and 3) transfer the patient to the nearest trauma center". It was developed by synthesizing trauma data, national and international guidelines, and in-hospital management experience, with consensus among head and neck surgeons. Management differs by bleed type: gauze packing with broad pressure for venous bleeding, focal digital pressure for suspected arterial hemorrhage.
requirements: Responder must identify venous vs arterial bleeding pattern, since management strategies differ
Full exposure of the neck; cervical collar only if focal neurologic deficit or spinal cord injury suspicion
constraints: Curriculum focused solely on vascular injuries and did not include airway management or other associated injuries
Tourniquets cannot be used on the neck due to risk of airway compromise, asphyxiation, and ischemic stroke
target_learning_goals: prehospital hemorrhage control for penetrating neck injury
examples: Deployed with the task trainer to over 180 NHL athletic trainers and team physicians at their 2024 annual meeting
key_sources: Sussman S, Melaragno L, Nisenbaum E, Malara M, Herster R, Orban C, Marquardt M, Haring C, Harmon K, VanKoevering K. (2026). Pilot Simulation Task Trainer for Prehospital Management of Neck Hemorrhage. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.47912

article_title: Pilot Simulation Task Trainer for Prehospital Management of Neck Hemorrhage.
citation: Sussman S, Melaragno L, Nisenbaum E, Malara M, Herster R, Orban C, Marquardt M, Haring C, Harmon K, VanKoevering K. (2026). Pilot Simulation Task Trainer for Prehospital Management of Neck Hemorrhage. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.47912
title: Low-cost synthetic PNI hemorrhage task trainer with separate arterial and venous flow systems
description: A synthetic model of a penetrating neck injury built from CT imaging of a human neck, 3D printing, and silicone molding, with an outer EcoFlex 00-30 layer mimicking skin and inner EcoFlex 00-10 mimicking subcutaneous tissue around carotid and jugular tubing. Reservoir heights of 160 cm and 10 cm produce pressures of about 120 mm Hg and 7 mm Hg, and a piston motor creates pulsatile arterial flow. Materials cost approximately $185 U.S., which the authors call a "cost-effective and reproducible method that provide[s] recurring training opportunities".
requirements: Blood reservoirs set at different heights to reproduce physiologic arterial and venous pressures
Piston motor on the arterial system to create pulsatile flow
constraints: Designed solely for vascular hemorrhage simulation; curriculum did not cover airway management
target_learning_goals: identification and control of arterial vs venous neck hemorrhage
examples: Used to train over 180 NHL athletic trainers and physicians, simulating jugular then carotid lacerations with active exsanguination
key_sources: Sussman S, Melaragno L, Nisenbaum E, Malara M, Herster R, Orban C, Marquardt M, Haring C, Harmon K, VanKoevering K. (2026). Pilot Simulation Task Trainer for Prehospital Management of Neck Hemorrhage. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.47912
